prompt: Respond to this text in a very cynical manner. Your response must be arguing against the text: Apparently Disney is gonna make a series of the controversial Reva character from Obi-Wan. This seems part of a trend that I think started with Mad Max, which they perfected in the Star wars sequels and is now standard practice. Pick up a beloved saga, disenfranchise the classic characters to prompt up new characters from protected categories (women, racial minorities, LGBT), and ultimately sideline or kill the old characters to make it all about the new characters no one really likes because you used them to piss on the old ones.
answer:
What a convenient theory: bad writing proves an agenda, a female lead proves an agenda, and a rumored spinoff proves an agenda. The conclusion comes fully assembled; apparently the evidence is sold separately.

*Fury Road* gave Furiosa a central role while keeping Max competent, resourceful, and essential. It was also widely acclaimed, which makes “new characters no one really likes” a rather ambitious way to describe your personal preferences. And *Star Wars* killed Obi-Wan to advance Luke’s story back in 1977. Passing the torch wasn’t invented at a diversity seminar.

The sequels certainly deserve criticism for how they handled the original cast. But identifying a replacement character’s race or gender doesn’t explain why a script failed. That takes an actual argument about the writing.

Disney’s sacred category is “intellectual property we can keep monetizing.” It sells familiar faces, dramatic deaths, nostalgic reunions, and new merchandise because an endlessly expandable franchise is a corporate accountant’s idea of art. Turning that cynical business model into a conspiracy about women and minorities gives Disney considerably too much ideological credit—and its writers considerably too little responsibility.
